claim: Individual retinal ganglion cell axons form clustered terminal boutons containing multiple active zones onto relay cell dendrites in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: In the mammalian visual system, individual retinal ganglion cell axons form clustered terminal boutons containing multiple active zones onto relay cell dendrites in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus.
evidence: This is a statement about the mature architecture of retinogeniculate connections, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The mature retinogeniculate architecture arises through the addition of release sites, which strengthens selected afferents while weaker inputs are pruned.
source: This mature architecture arises through the addition of release sites, which strengthens selected afferents while weaker inputs are pruned.
evidence: This statement describes a developmental mechanism supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Following eye-opening, spontaneous activity and visual experience promote synaptic refinement and bouton clustering after binocular inputs have segregated.
source: Following eye-opening, spontaneous activity and visual experience promote synaptic refinement and bouton clustering after binocular inputs have segregated.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work in the field.

claim: Individual retinogeniculate boutons begin forming multiple nearby presynaptic active zones during the first postnatal week.
source: Using volumetric super-resolution single-molecule localization microscopy and electron microscopy, we found that individual retinogeniculate boutons begin forming multiple nearby presynaptic active zones during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from STORM and EM imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both eyes generate multi-active-zone (mAZ) inputs throughout refinement.
source: Both eyes generate these 'multi-active-zone' (mAZ) inputs throughout refinement, but the dominant eye forms more numerous mAZ contacts, each with more active zones and larger vesicle pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from STORM imaging across developmental time points.

claim: The dominant eye forms more numerous mAZ contacts, each with more active zones and larger vesicle pools.
source: Both eyes generate these 'multi-active-zone' (mAZ) inputs throughout refinement, but the dominant eye forms more numerous mAZ contacts, each with more active zones and larger vesicle pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of mAZ density, AZ number, and vesicle pool volume presented in the results.

claim: At the height of competition (postnatal day 4), the non-dominant-eye projection adds many single-active-zone synapses.
source: At the height of competition (postnatal day 4), the non-dominant-eye projection adds many single-active-zone synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density measurements at P4 showing increased sAZ synapses from the non-dominant eye.

claim: Mutants with abnormal cholinergic retinal waves still form mAZ inputs but develop fewer synapses overall.
source: Mutants with abnormal cholinergic retinal waves still form mAZ inputs but develop fewer synapses overall and show reduced synaptic clustering in projections from both eyes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from β2KO mice showing mAZ formation but reduced synapse density.

claim: Mutants with abnormal cholinergic retinal waves show reduced synaptic clustering in projections from both eyes.
source: Mutants with abnormal cholinergic retinal waves still form mAZ inputs but develop fewer synapses overall and show reduced synaptic clustering in projections from both eyes.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis data from β2KO mice.

claim: Eye-specific differences in release site addition correlate with axonal segregation outcomes during retinogeniculate refinement.
source: Together, these findings reveal eye-specific differences in release site addition that correlate with axonal segregation outcomes during retinogeniculate refinement.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neighboring synaptic inputs play critical computational roles in learning, memory, and sensory processing underlying cognition and behavior.
source: Through biophysical signal integration mechanisms, neighboring synaptic inputs play critical computational roles in learning, memory, and sensory processing underlying cognition and behavior (Mel et al., 2017; Kastellakis and Poirazi, 2019; Winnubst and Lohmann, 2012; Leighton and Lohmann, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During circuit development, both spontaneous and sensory-driven neural activity regulate synaptic clustering.
source: During circuit development, both spontaneous and sensory-driven neural activity regulate synaptic clustering, stabilizing some synapses and eliminating others to establish mature connectivity patterns (Winnubst and Lohmann, 2012; Leighton and Lohmann, 2016; Kirchner and Gjorgjieva, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Boutons within the terminal arbors of individual retinogeniculate axons cluster progressively over development.
source: Over development, boutons within the terminal arbors of individual retinogeniculate axons cluster progressively (Bickford et al., 2010; Monavarfeshani et al., 2018; Hong et al., 2014; Mason, 1982), creating multiple synaptic contacts onto individual postsynaptic targets (Hamos et al., 1987; Hammer et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Developing retinal ganglion cell boutons add presynaptic release sites such that some mature retinogeniculate terminals contain several dozen active zones.
source: Concurrently, developing retinal ganglion cell (RGC) boutons add presynaptic release sites such that some mature retinogeniculate terminals contain several dozen active zones (AZs) (Morgan et al., 2016; Budisantoso et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The formation of clustered boutons with multiple release sites subserves a critical 'driver' function of retinogeniculate input.
source: The formation of clustered boutons with multiple release sites subserves a critical 'driver' function of retinogeniculate input (Sherman and Guillery, 1998; Guillery and Sherman, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Retinogeniculate bouton clustering depends on visual experience.
source: Retinogeniculate bouton clustering depends on visual experience, and dark-rearing after eye-opening reduces clustering within individual axon arbors (Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dark-rearing after eye-opening reduces clustering within individual axon arbors.
source: Retinogeniculate bouton clustering depends on visual experience, and dark-rearing after eye-opening reduces clustering within individual axon arbors (Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During early axon ingrowth, individual RGCs extend sparse side branches in the incorrect eye-specific territory.
source: During early axon ingrowth, individual RGCs extend sparse side branches in the incorrect eye-specific territory (Sretavan and Shatz, 1984; Sretavan and Shatz, 1986; Dhande et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transient branches form synapses that contain fewer presynaptic vesicles than those made by the same axon in the correct eye-specific domain.
source: These transient branches form synapses that contain fewer presynaptic vesicles than those made by the same axon in the correct eye-specific domain (Campbell and Shatz, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: While many RGC inputs are pruned, the remaining inputs strengthen by adding release sites.
source: Functional recordings after eye-opening show that while many RGC inputs are pruned, the remaining inputs strengthen by adding release sites (Chen and Regehr, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Release site addition leads to glutamate spillover and cross-talk between RGC inputs that increases postsynaptic relay neuron excitability.
source: This leads to glutamate spillover and cross-talk between RGC inputs that increases postsynaptic relay neuron excitability (Hauser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dominant-eye synapses contain more total vesicles and have more vesicles near the AZ (putative docking) compared with non-dominant-eye synapses.
source: In a previous study from our laboratory, we used volumetric stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM), anterograde tract tracing, and immunohistochemical labeling of synaptic proteins to show that dominant-eye synapses contain more total vesicles and have more vesicles near the AZ (putative docking) compared with non-dominant-eye synapses (Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Projections from each eye form a subset of retinogeniculate inputs in which several (2–4) AZs share a common cluster of presynaptic vesicles.
source: We found that projections from each eye form a subset of retinogeniculate inputs in which several (2–4) AZs share a common cluster of presynaptic vesicles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the reanalysis of STORM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During eye-specific synaptic competition, the dominant-eye projection formed more mAZ inputs, each with more AZs and a larger presynaptic vesicle pool compared to the non-dominant-eye projection.
source: During eye-specific synaptic competition, the dominant-eye projection formed more mAZ inputs, each with more AZs and a larger presynaptic vesicle pool compared to the non-dominant-eye projection.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from STORM imaging.

claim: The dominant eye had higher vesicle signal at sAZ inputs.
source: Similarly, the dominant eye had higher vesicle signal at sAZ inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of VGluT2 volume.

claim: At postnatal day 4, the non-dominant-eye formed numerous sAZ inputs, equalizing the global synapse density between the two eyes.
source: At the peak of synaptic competition midway through the first postnatal week (postnatal day 4), the non-dominant-eye formed numerous sAZ inputs, equalizing the global synapse density between the two eyes.
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density measurements at P4.

claim: Eye-specific AZ patterns were disrupted in a mutant mouse line with abnormal stage II cholinergic retinal waves and retinogeniculate segregation defects.
source: These eye-specific AZ patterns were disrupted in a mutant mouse line with abnormal stage II cholinergic retinal waves and retinogeniculate segregation defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from β2KO mice.

claim: STORM revealed two classes of retinogeniculate inputs distinguished by active zone (AZ) number.
source: By analyzing synapses in the contralateral dLGN from 18 mice across three ages and two genotypes (Supplementary file 1), STORM revealed two classes of retinogeniculate inputs distinguished by active zone (AZ) number (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data and Figure 1B.

claim: Most mAZ inputs contained two AZs (~70–90%, varying with age, genotype, and eye-of-origin).
source: Most mAZ inputs contained two AZs (~70–90%, varying with age, genotype, and eye-of-origin); smaller proportions contained three AZs (~10–20%) or four or more AZs (<5%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mAZ inputs.

claim: EM images confirmed the presence of individual retinogeniculate boutons with multiple active zones.
source: EM images confirmed the presence of individual retinogeniculate boutons with multiple active zones, consistent with our STORM data (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Previous EM reconstructions of retinogeniculate inputs reported no evidence of RGC bouton convergence at the end of the first postnatal week.
source: Previous EM reconstructions of retinogeniculate inputs reported no evidence of RGC bouton convergence at the end of the first postnatal week (Monavarfeshani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: mAZ inputs in STORM images are single RGC terminals that house several closely spaced release sites.
source: Together, these results suggest that mAZ inputs in STORM images are single RGC terminals that house several closely spaced release sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on EM data and prior EM reconstructions.

claim: Anterograde tracing labeled >97% of retinogeniculate synapses at P4 and P8.
source: Binocular CTB control injections showed that anterograde tracing labeled >97% of retinogeniculate synapses at P4 and P8, ensuring accurate eye-specific assignment (Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments from a previous publication.

claim: The density of CTB(+) mAZ inputs tended to be higher than CTB(−) mAZ inputs in WT mice.
source: After false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons within each age and genotype (see Quantification and statistical analysis; p(adj) values shown in all figures and Supplementary file 2), we found that the density of CTB(+) mAZ inputs tended to be higher than CTB(−) mAZ inputs in WT mice (Figure 2C, top left).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mAZ input fraction was significantly higher for CTB(+) dominant-eye inputs at P4 and P8.
source: Consistent with this trend, the mAZ input fraction (% of all inputs) was significantly higher for CTB(+) dominant-eye inputs at P4 and P8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: β2KO mice also developed differences in mAZ input density favoring the dominant-eye.
source: β2KO mice also developed differences in mAZ input density favoring the dominant-eye (Figure 2C, bottom left; Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For WT sAZ synapses, the dominant eye had a significantly higher synapse density at P2.
source: For WT sAZ synapses, the dominant eye had a significantly higher synapse density at P2 [p(adj) = 0.026, Cohen's d = 5.31] and trended higher at P8 [p(adj) = 0.072, Cohen's d = 2.73].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of synapse density data.

claim: At P4, sAZ synapse density was equivalent between the eyes in WT mice.
source: At P4, however, sAZ synapse density was equivalent between the eyes (Figure 2C, top right; Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: This pattern resulted from non-dominant-eye sAZ synapse addition, which equalized the global input density between the eyes at P4.
source: This pattern resulted from non-dominant-eye sAZ synapse addition, which equalized the global input density between the eyes at P4 as we reported previously (5/95% confidence interval, −0.014 to 0.011 synapses/μm3).
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density data and confidence intervals.

claim: In β2KO mice at P4, the non-dominant-eye formed fewer sAZ synapses.
source: In β2KO mice at P4, the non-dominant-eye formed fewer sAZ synapses (Figure 2C, bottom right; see Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: β2KO mice with disrupted retinal activity maintain a higher mAZ input fraction in the dominant-eye projection, but sAZ synapse addition is reduced at the peak of competition.
source: Thus, β2KO mice with disrupted retinal activity maintain a higher mAZ input fraction in the dominant-eye projection, but sAZ synapse addition is reduced at the peak of competition.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented for β2KO mice.

claim: In WT mice, both mAZ and sAZ inputs showed significant eye-specific volume differences in the middle of eye-specific competition at P4.
source: In WT mice, both mAZ (Figure 3A, left) and sAZ (Figure 3B, left) inputs showed significant eye-specific volume differences in the middle of eye-specific competition at P4.
evidence: This claim is supported by VGluT2 volume measurements shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: At P4 in WT mice, the median VGluT2 cluster volume in dominant-eye mAZ inputs was ~3.55 ± 1.3 μm3 larger (mean ± SE) than that of non-dominant-eye inputs.
source: At this age in WT mice, the median VGluT2 cluster volume in dominant-eye mAZ inputs was ~3.55 ± 1.3 μm3 larger (mean ± SE) than that of non-dominant-eye inputs (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: β2KO mice showed a smaller ~1.9 ± 1.1 μm3 (mean ± SE) volume difference between median eye-specific mAZ inputs at P4.
source: In contrast, β2KO mice showed a smaller ~1.9 ± 1.1 μm3 (mean ± SE) volume difference between median eye-specific mAZ inputs at the same age (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For sAZ synapses at P4, the magnitudes of eye-specific differences in median VGluT2 volume (mean ± SE) were ~2.1 ± 1.0 μm3 in WT.
source: For sAZ synapses at P4, the magnitudes of eye-specific differences in median VGluT2 volume (mean ± SE) were ~2.1 ± 1.0 μm3 in WT (Figure 3B, left) and ~1.5 ± 1.1 in β2KO mice (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both mAZ and sAZ vesicle pool volumes are larger for the dominant eye, with the largest eye-specific differences seen for mAZ inputs in WT mice.
source: Thus, both mAZ and sAZ vesicle pool volumes are larger for the dominant eye, with the largest eye-specific differences seen for mAZ inputs in WT mice (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the VGluT2 volume data.

claim: In WT mice at P4, dominant-eye inputs showed greater vesicle volume per AZ than non-dominant inputs, in both mAZ and sAZ terminals.
source: In WT mice at P4, dominant-eye inputs showed greater vesicle volume per AZ than non-dominant inputs, in both mAZ and sAZ terminals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, left; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of VGluT2 volume within a 70-nm shell around AZs.

claim: Eye-specific differences in vesicle volume per AZ were absent in β2KO mice.
source: These eye-specific differences were absent in β2KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, right; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When comparing mAZ and sAZ inputs from the same eye, vesicle volume per AZ was similar across all ages and genotypes.
source: However, when comparing mAZ and sAZ inputs from the same eye, vesicle volume per AZ was similar across all ages and genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vesicle docking favors the dominant eye.
source: This confirms our previous finding that vesicle docking favors the dominant eye (Zhang et al., 2023) and shows that AZs formed by a single eye have similar docking levels in both their mAZ and sAZ terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and a previous publication.

claim: AZs formed by a single eye have similar docking levels in both their mAZ and sAZ terminals.
source: This confirms our previous finding that vesicle docking favors the dominant eye (Zhang et al., 2023) and shows that AZs formed by a single eye have similar docking levels in both their mAZ and sAZ terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the vesicle docking measurements.

claim: In both WT and β2KO mice, mAZ inputs contained an average of two to three Bassoon clusters (separate AZs) in the first postnatal week.
source: In both WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and β2KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), mAZ inputs contained an average of two to three Bassoon clusters (separate AZs) in the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: In WT mice, CTB(+) dominant-eye mAZ inputs contained more AZs than CTB(−) non-dominant-eye mAZ inputs at P4 and P8.
source: In WT mice, CTB(+) dominant-eye mAZ inputs contained more AZs than CTB(−) non-dominant-eye mAZ inputs at P4 and P8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: This maturation was delayed until P8 in β2KO mice.
source: This maturation was delayed until P8 in β2KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: For CTB(+) dominant-eye inputs in both genotypes at P4, vesicle pool volume correlated positively with AZ number.
source: For CTB(+) dominant-eye inputs in both genotypes at P4, vesicle pool volume correlated positively with AZ number (Figure 3C; Pearson correlation coefficients: WT [0.99] and β2KO [0.95]).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A similar, but weaker correlation was observed for CTB(−) non-dominant-eye inputs.
source: A similar, but weaker correlation was observed for CTB(−) non-dominant-eye inputs (Pearson correlation coefficients: WT [0.97] and β2KO [0.90]).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Dividing the total presynaptic VGluT2 volume by the AZ number revealed a consistent vesicle volume per AZ for both sAZ and mAZ inputs.
source: Dividing the total presynaptic VGluT2 volume by the AZ number revealed a consistent vesicle volume per AZ for both sAZ and mAZ inputs (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Presynaptic vesicle pool volume scales with AZ number for each eye-specific input, while a dominant-eye bias persists throughout development.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that presynaptic vesicle pool volume scales with AZ number for each eye-specific input, while a dominant-eye bias persists throughout development.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the vesicle pool volume and AZ number data.

claim: Eye-specific competition is thought to involve stabilization of coactive, neighboring inputs from the same eye and elimination of out-of-sync inputs from the opposite eye.
source: Eye-specific competition is thought to involve stabilization of coactive, neighboring inputs from the same eye and elimination of out-of-sync inputs from the opposite eye (Assali et al., 2014; Fassier and Nicol, 2021; Penn et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Axon refinement depends on the relative strength of neurotransmission between competing inputs.
source: Because axon refinement depends on the relative strength of neurotransmission between competing inputs (Koch et al., 2011; Assali et al., 2017; Fredj et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2005; Rahman et al., 2020; Munz et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 1998; Matsumoto et al., 2024), mAZ inputs with multiple release sites could help stabilize nearby like-eye inputs (Rahman et al., 2020; Yasuda et al., 2021; Louail et al., 2020; Kutsarova et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: mAZ inputs with multiple release sites could help stabilize nearby like-eye inputs.
source: Because axon refinement depends on the relative strength of neurotransmission between competing inputs (Koch et al., 2011; Assali et al., 2017; Fredj et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2005; Rahman et al., 2020; Munz et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 1998; Matsumoto et al., 2024), mAZ inputs with multiple release sites could help stabilize nearby like-eye inputs (Rahman et al., 2020; Yasuda et al., 2021; Louail et al., 2020; Kutsarova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on prior work and the current findings.

claim: sAZ synapses were often found nearby other inputs from the same eye.
source: sAZ synapses were often found nearby other inputs from the same eye (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: The largest differences in clustering occurred within a 1- to 2-μm search distance.
source: The largest differences occurred within a 1- to 2-μm search distance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B), and so we chose a 1.5-μm cutoff from the edge of each mAZ input to designate it 'clustered' if at least one neighboring sAZ synapse lay within this distance and 'isolated' if none did (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: No significant clustering was detected when sAZ and mAZ inputs originated from opposite eyes.
source: No significant clustering was detected when sAZ and mAZ inputs originated from opposite eyes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: At the peak of competition in WT mice (P4), more than 65% of both mAZ and sAZ inputs were clustered for both eyes.
source: At the peak of competition in WT mice (P4), more than 65% of both mAZ and sAZ inputs were clustered for both eyes, while this proportion fell to ~50% in β2KO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the WT dominant-eye projection, the fractions of clustered mAZ and sAZ inputs were similar at each age.
source: In the WT dominant-eye projection, the fractions of clustered mAZ and sAZ inputs were similar at each age (Figure 4C, top left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For the non-dominant-eye projection, there were slightly more clustered mAZ inputs compared to clustered sAZ inputs at P4.
source: For the non-dominant-eye projection, however, there were slightly more clustered mAZ inputs compared to clustered sAZ inputs at P4 (Figure 4C, bottom left panel), the age when this eye adds sAZ synapses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: β2KO mice showed no difference between mAZ and sAZ clustering at any age.
source: β2KO mice showed no difference between mAZ and sAZ clustering at any age (Figure 4C, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In WT mice at P4 and P8, clustered mAZ inputs from both eyes had marginally more neighboring sAZ synapses than did clustered sAZ synapses.
source: Additionally, in WT mice at P4 and P8, clustered mAZ inputs from both eyes had marginally more neighboring sAZ synapses than did clustered sAZ synapses (Figure 4D, left); this enrichment was absent in β2KO mice (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: While most retinogeniculate synapses lie within 1.5 μm of another like-eye input, WT mice show a tendency toward forming more synapses near mAZ inputs during synaptic competition.
source: Thus, while most retinogeniculate synapses lie within 1.5 μm of another like-eye input, WT mice show a tendency toward forming more synapses near mAZ inputs during synaptic competition.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the clustering data.

claim: Clustered mAZ inputs in P4 WT mice were also closer together than isolated mAZ inputs.
source: Clustered mAZ inputs in P4 WT mice were also closer together than isolated mAZ inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements.

claim: Clustered mAZ inputs formed by the dominant eye were ~32% closer to the nearest like-eye clustered mAZ input compared to isolated mAZ inputs.
source: Clustered mAZ inputs formed by the dominant eye were ~32% closer to the nearest like-eye clustered mAZ input compared to isolated mAZ inputs (Figure 5A, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the non-dominant-eye projection, clustered mAZ inputs were ~55% closer together compared to isolated mAZ inputs.
source: In the non-dominant-eye projection, clustered mAZ inputs were ~55% closer together compared to isolated mAZ inputs (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Once segregation was complete at P8, distances between clustered and isolated mAZ inputs were more similar.
source: Once segregation was complete at P8, distances between clustered and isolated mAZ inputs were more similar (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In β2KO mice, distances between isolated and clustered mAZ inputs and their nearest clustered mAZ neighbor did not differ for either eye at P4 or P8.
source: In β2KO mice, distances between isolated and clustered mAZ inputs and their nearest clustered mAZ neighbor did not differ for either eye at P4 or P8 (Figure 5, right panels; Figure 5—figure supplement 1, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: These patterns are consistent with sAZ synapse addition when mAZ inputs are in close proximity during competition.
source: These patterns are consistent with sAZ synapse addition when mAZ inputs are in close proximity during competition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distance and clustering data.

claim: Across ages and genotypes, vesicle pool volume was similar for near and far sAZ synapses in both eyes.
source: Across ages and genotypes, vesicle pool volume was similar for near and far sAZ synapses in both eyes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by VGluT2 volume measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vesicle pool size in sAZ synapses appears independent of their proximity to mAZ inputs.
source: Thus, vesicle pool size in sAZ synapses appears independent of their proximity to mAZ inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VGluT2 volume measurements.

claim: Before eye-opening, RGC axons from both eyes formed terminals with either multiple active zones (mAZ inputs) or a single active zone (sAZ synapses).
source: Before eye-opening, RGC axons from both eyes formed terminals with either multiple active zones (mAZ inputs) or a single active zone (sAZ synapses).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the STORM data.

claim: EM of dAPEX2-labeled ipsilateral RGC inputs revealed individual boutons with multiple active zones.
source: EM of dAPEX2-labeled ipsilateral RGC inputs revealed individual boutons with multiple active zones.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data.

claim: Prior EM studies in mice showed no clustering from neighboring RGC boutons at postnatal day 8.
source: Prior EM studies in mice showed no clustering from neighboring RGC boutons at postnatal day 8 (Bickford et al., 2010; Monavarfeshani et al., 2018), suggesting the mAZ inputs seen in STORM images are single boutons containing multiple release sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During competition, the dominant eye projection generated more of these mAZ inputs, each with more active zones and larger vesicle pools than the non-dominant eye.
source: During competition, the dominant eye projection generated more of these mAZ inputs, each with more active zones and larger vesicle pools than the non-dominant eye.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the quantitative data.

claim: We observed a linear relationship between presynaptic vesicle signal volume and active zone number.
source: We observed a linear relationship between presynaptic vesicle signal volume and active zone number, suggesting that release site addition and vesicle pool expansion may be linked during input maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Release site addition and vesicle pool expansion may be linked during input maturation.
source: We observed a linear relationship between presynaptic vesicle signal volume and active zone number, suggesting that release site addition and vesicle pool expansion may be linked during input maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the correlation data.

claim: Functional recordings indicate that release site addition is the primary driver of retinogeniculate input strengthening after eye-opening.
source: Functional recordings indicate that release site addition is the primary driver of retinogeniculate input strengthening after eye-opening (Chen and Regehr, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Eye-specific differences in release site addition at individual terminals emerge at the earliest stages of binocular refinement.
source: Our findings reveal that eye-specific differences in release site addition at individual terminals emerge at the earliest stages of binocular refinement.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current findings.

claim: Ipsilateral RGC axons are delayed in entering the dLGN until after contralateral inputs have already innervated the nucleus.
source: Ipsilateral RGC axons are delayed in entering the dLGN until after contralateral inputs have already innervated the nucleus (Godement et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Despite their late arrival, these axons competed by forming numerous sAZ inputs, which equalized the overall input density between the eyes in the future contralateral eye domain at postnatal day 4 (P4).
source: Despite their late arrival, these axons competed by forming numerous sAZ inputs, which equalized the overall input density between the eyes in the future contralateral eye domain at postnatal day 4 (P4).
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density data.

claim: Most of these synapses formed nearby other like-eye neighbors and were enriched near mAZ inputs.
source: Most of these synapses formed nearby other like-eye neighbors and were enriched near mAZ inputs, supporting the idea of release site addition at strong synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering data.

claim: Neighboring sAZ synapses could ultimately mature into mAZ inputs as release sites are added and vesicle pools expand.
source: Neighboring sAZ synapses could ultimately mature into mAZ inputs as release sites are added and vesicle pools expand.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the clustering and maturation data.

claim: Distance analysis showed that clustered mAZ boutons were closer together than isolated mAZ boutons.
source: Distance analysis showed that clustered mAZ boutons were closer together than isolated mAZ boutons, further supporting release site addition near strong neighboring inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements.

claim: It remains unknown whether nearby mAZ inputs originate from the same RGC.
source: It remains unknown, however, whether nearby mAZ inputs originate from the same RGC.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the current study.

claim: Nearby mAZ inputs within individual RGC arbors could promote release site addition via intrinsic mechanisms that scale with release site number, such as increased presynaptic calcium entry or surface delivery of synaptogenic molecules via presynaptic release.
source: Nearby mAZ inputs within individual RGC arbors could promote release site addition via intrinsic mechanisms that scale with release site number, such as increased presynaptic calcium entry or surface delivery of synaptogenic molecules via presynaptic release.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Boutons with multiple release sites could also trigger non-cell-autonomous signaling mechanisms that stabilize neighboring inputs from the same eye.
source: Boutons with multiple release sites could also trigger non-cell-autonomous signaling mechanisms that stabilize neighboring inputs from the same eye (Rahman et al., 2020; Louail et al., 2020; Kutsarova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Release site addition increases extracellular glutamate concentration and promotes spillover onto adjacent synapses, which enhances the excitability of developing relay cells.
source: Release site addition increases extracellular glutamate concentration and promotes spillover onto adjacent synapses, which enhances the excitability of developing relay cells (Hauser et al., 2014) and could contribute to long-term synaptic plasticity evoked by high-frequency spiking in retinal wave bursts (Mooney et al., 1993; Ziburkus et al., 2009; Butts et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Release site addition and local bouton clustering may act in tandem to stabilize coactive inputs.
source: Consequently, release site addition and local bouton clustering may act in tandem to stabilize coactive inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current findings and prior work.

claim: Genetic deletions of VGluT2 or RIM1 proteins in ipsilaterally projecting RGCs decreased presynaptic vesicle release and prevented retraction of contralateral RGC axons from the ipsilateral territory.
source: Genetic deletions of VGluT2 or RIM1 proteins in ipsilaterally projecting RGCs decreased presynaptic vesicle release and prevented retraction of contralateral RGC axons from the ipsilateral territory (Koch et al., 2011; Assali et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: One downstream mediator of synaptic punishment is JAK2 kinase, which is phosphorylated in less active synapses.
source: One downstream mediator of synaptic punishment is JAK2 kinase, which is phosphorylated in less active synapses (Yasuda et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Disruption of JAK2 signaling prevents axon retraction (punishment) during competition.
source: Similar to neurotransmission mutant phenotypes, disruption of JAK2 signaling prevents axon retraction (punishment) during competition (Yasuda et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: β2KO mice showed significant defects in synapse addition during the first postnatal week.
source: β2KO mice showed significant defects in synapse addition during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density data from β2KO mice.

claim: mAZs still formed with similar overall ratios as in WT controls in β2KO mice.
source: mAZs still formed with similar overall ratios as in WT controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3) and eye-specific differences in vesicle pool size still emerged.
evidence: This claim is supported by mAZ fraction data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: β2KO mice failed to form many sAZ synapses at the height of competition (P4), particularly in the late-arriving non-dominant (ipsilateral)-eye projection.
source: However, β2KO mice failed to form many sAZ synapses at the height of competition (P4), particularly in the late-arriving non-dominant (ipsilateral)-eye projection.
evidence: This claim is supported by synapse density data from β2KO mice.

claim: The failure to add synapses could explain the observation that synaptic clustering was reduced and more inputs formed in isolation in the mutants compared to controls.
source: The failure to add synapses could explain the observation that synaptic clustering was reduced and more inputs formed in isolation in the mutants compared to controls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synapse density and clustering data from β2KO mice.

claim: Retinogeniculate synapses undergo postsynaptic strengthening and weakening through potentiation and depression mediated by AMPARs and NMDARs.
source: Retinogeniculate synapses undergo postsynaptic strengthening and weakening through potentiation and depression mediated by AMPARs and NMDARs (Mooney et al., 1993; Ziburkus et al., 2009; Butts et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After eye-specific segregation, spontaneous retinal activity is required for postsynaptic AMPAR insertion, synaptic strengthening, and elimination of weaker inputs.
source: After eye-specific segregation, spontaneous retinal activity is required for postsynaptic AMPAR insertion, synaptic strengthening, and elimination of weaker inputs (Hooks and Chen, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Continued maintenance of segregation depends on calcium influx into relay neurons via L-type calcium channels.
source: Continued maintenance of segregation depends on calcium influx into relay neurons via L-type calcium channels, further implicating postsynaptic signaling in late-stage refinement (Dilger et al., 2015; Cork et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ipsilaterally projecting RGCs have distinct gene expression profiles that specify axon guidance and may further support eye-specific synaptic targeting.
source: Ipsilaterally projecting RGCs have distinct gene expression profiles that specify axon guidance and may further support eye-specific synaptic targeting (Fernández-Nogales et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spontaneous retinal activity may permit axons to read out molecular regulators of synaptogenesis.
source: Spontaneous retinal activity may permit axons to read out molecular regulators of synaptogenesis, as previously shown for RGC axon retraction (Nicol et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Early synaptic clustering during retinogeniculate development resembles other circuits where neural activity guides competitive synaptic and axonal remodeling.
source: Early synaptic clustering during retinogeniculate development resembles other circuits where neural activity guides competitive synaptic and axonal remodeling.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the current findings and knowledge of other systems.

claim: At the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), motor neuron terminals compete for control of a postsynaptic muscle fiber; a single motor axon input strengthens while competing axons are eliminated.
source: At the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), motor neuron terminals compete for control of a postsynaptic muscle fiber; a single motor axon input strengthens while competing axons are eliminated (Balice-Gordon et al., 1993; Gan and Lichtman, 1998; Wyatt and Balice-Gordon, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Competition at the NMJ depends on inter-synaptic distance, with motor axons losing connections located near stronger competing synapses.
source: Competition at the NMJ depends on inter-synaptic distance, with motor axons losing connections located near stronger competing synapses (Balice-Gordon et al., 1993; Gan and Lichtman, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: As winning terminals are enlarged, presynaptic release site addition maintains a consistent density of Bassoon clusters (~2–3/μm2).
source: As winning terminals are enlarged, presynaptic release site addition maintains a consistent density of Bassoon clusters (~2–3/μm2) (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neighboring inputs with weaker synaptic transmission are selectively eliminated at the NMJ.
source: Neighboring inputs with weaker synaptic transmission are selectively eliminated (Balice-Gordon and Lichtman, 1994; Buffelli et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Competing motor axons differ in their release probabilities early in development.
source: Competing motor axons differ in their release probabilities early in development (Kopp et al., 2000), suggesting that presynaptic efficacy triggers local 'stabilization' signals in winners and 'punishment' signals in losers (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Presynaptic agrin release stabilizes postsynaptic receptor clusters by counteracting the destabilizing, dispersal effects of acetylcholine release.
source: Presynaptic agrin release stabilizes postsynaptic receptor clusters by counteracting the destabilizing, dispersal effects of acetylcholine release, emphasizing the importance of early presynaptic transmission in postsynaptic stabilization (Misgeld et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the developing cerebellum, Purkinje cells initially receive inputs from multiple climbing fibers (CFs) during the first postnatal week.
source: Similarly, in the developing cerebellum, Purkinje cells initially receive inputs from multiple climbing fibers (CFs) during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of cerebellar development.

claim: One winning CF emerges and consolidates its synaptic inputs, while losing CFs are pruned.
source: Subsequently, one winning CF emerges and consolidates its synaptic inputs, while losing CFs are pruned (Hashimoto and Kano, 2013; Bosman and Konnerth, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The winning CF input strengthens by adding presynaptic release sites, which increases multivesicular release and elevates glutamate concentration in the synaptic cleft.
source: Here again, the winning input strengthens by adding presynaptic release sites, which increases multivesicular release and elevates glutamate concentration in the synaptic cleft (Hashimoto and Kano, 2003; Nitta et al., 2025; Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Postsynaptic ultrastructural and molecular changes occur several days later as dominant CF inputs potentiate and losing CF inputs depress.
source: Postsynaptic ultrastructural and molecular changes occur several days later as dominant CF inputs potentiate and losing CF inputs depress (Nitta et al., 2025; Bosman et al., 2008; Ohtsuki and Hirano, 2008) through spike-timing-dependent remodeling (Lorenzetto et al., 2009; Kawamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Across these models, the earliest distinguishing feature between competing inputs is relative presynaptic transmission strength.
source: Across these models, the earliest distinguishing feature between competing inputs is relative presynaptic transmission strength.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on comparisons across different systems.

claim: Release-site addition may be a conserved mechanism that biases synaptic refinement outcomes across developing neural circuits.
source: Thus, release-site addition may be a conserved mechanism that biases synaptic refinement outcomes across developing neural circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on comparisons across different systems.
